citations.quote:
Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$
be $C^2$. Let $p,m\in\mathbb N$ with zero allowed; when the target
dimension is positive, let $h:U\to\mathbb R^p$ and
$g=(g_1,\ldots,g_m):U\to\mathbb R^m$ be componentwise $C^2$, and when it
is zero use the unique empty map. The $C^2$ convention for positive
dimensions is [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]].
The smooth inequality program is to minimize $f(x)$ subject to
$h(x)=0$ and $g_i(x)\le0$ for every $i$. Its feasible set is
$C=\{x\in U:h(x)=0,\ g_i(x)\le0\ (1\le i\le m)\}$. A feasible point $x_*$ is
a local minimizer if some open neighborhood $V$ of $x_*$ satisfies
$f(x_*)\le f(y)$ for every $y\in C\cap V$.

At a feasible $x$, the active set is
$I(x)=\{i:g_i(x)=0\}$. The Bouligand tangent cone and linearized cone are,
respectively,
$$
T_C(x)=\{d:\exists\,t_k>0,\ t_k\downarrow0,\ d_k\to d,\ x+t_kd_k\in C\},
$$
and
$$
\mathcal L_C(x)=\{d:Dh(x)d=0,\ Dg_i(x)d\le0\text{ for every }i\in I(x)\}.
$$
Gradients are column vectors and $Dg_i(x)d=\nabla g_i(x)^Td$.

The linear independence constraint qualification (LICQ) holds at $x$ when the rows of $Dh(x)$ together with
$\{\nabla g_i(x)^T:i\in I(x)\}$ are linearly independent. MFCQ holds at $x$
when $Dh(x)$ has full row rank (its rows are linearly independent) and there is $w\in\ker Dh(x)$ with
$Dg_i(x)w<0$ for every active $i$; the latter condition is vacuous if
$I(x)=\varnothing$. Here full row rank for a matrix with zero rows is
understood vacuously.

The Mangasarian–Fromovitz constraint qualification (MFCQ) is the condition
just stated. The Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) system is the stationarity,
feasibility, dual-feasibility, and complementarity system below.

For $\nu\in\mathbb R^p$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb R^m$, the Lagrangian and KKT
system are
$$
L(x,\nu,\lambda)=f(x)+\nu^Th(x)+\lambda^Tg(x),
$$
$$
h(x)=0,\quad g(x)\le0,\quad \lambda\ge0,\quad \lambda_i g_i(x)=0\ (1\le i\le m),\quad \nabla_xL(x,\nu,\lambda)=0.
$$
The critical cone for a KKT tuple is
$\mathcal K(x,\nu,\lambda)=\mathcal L_C(x)\cap
\{d:\nabla f(x)^Td=0\}$. These definitions use the differentiability and
gradient conventions of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]],
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].

routine_steps.claim: Differentiability at $x$ gives the affine first-order models $h(x)+Dh(x)p$ and $g(x)+Dg(x)p$; the positive-definite quadratic model is finite for every $p\in\mathbb R^n$. Thus the displayed feasible set is a well-defined polyhedron, possibly empty.

For an active affine inequality, the multiplier convention in the Lagrangian contributes $Dg_i(x)^T\lambda_i$ to stationarity, while complementarity is $\lambda_i(g_i(x)+Dg_i(x)p)=0$. Hence the stated KKT tuple uses the same sign convention as [F1].

Statement inherits zero equality/inequality dimensions from the program definition; proof step 1.1 remains valid for empty maps.

routine_steps.claim: For any scalar $s=\lambda_i+\rho g_i(x)$, the identity $([s]_+)^2-\lambda_i^2=(s^2-\lambda_i^2)$ when $s>0$ expands to $2\rho\lambda_i g_i+\rho^2g_i^2$; when $s\le0$, $[s]_+=0$. This gives the two stated inequality branches and shows they agree in value at their boundary.

Differentiating the equality branch gives multiplier update $\nu+\rho h(x)$. On the positive inequality branch, differentiating its summand gives $[\lambda_i+\rho g_i(x)]_+Dg_i(x)^T$; on the nonpositive branch it gives zero. Thus the projected update is nonnegative and is consistent with the displayed piecewise gradient.

derivations.claim: Suppose $K\binom{z}{\mu}=0$. Its lower block gives $Az=0$, so $z\in\ker A$; multiplying the upper block $Hz+A^T\mu=0$ by $z^T$ gives $z^THz=0$. Positive definiteness on $\ker A$ forces $z=0$.

With $z=0$, the upper block gives $A^T\mu=0$. Full row rank of $A$ means $A^T$ is injective, so $\mu=0$. Thus the square matrix $K$ has trivial kernel and is nonsingular; when $r=0$, the same argument says $H$ has trivial kernel.

Use the smooth nonlinear program convention of
[[def-inequality-constrained-program-and-kkt-geometry]]: minimize a $C^2$
objective $f:U\to\mathbb R$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, subject to
$h(x)=0$ and componentwise $g(x)\le0$. Fix a current point $x\in U$ and a
symmetric positive-definite matrix $B\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$. The
**SQP quadratic subproblem** is
$$\min_{p\in\mathbb R^n}\quad \nabla f(x)^Tp+\tfrac12p^TBp \quad\text{subject to}\quad h(x)+Dh(x)p=0,\quad g(x)+Dg(x)p\le0.$$
The variable $p$ is the proposed displacement. Its feasible set is the
polyhedron defined by the displayed affine constraints. A constraint index
$i$ is **active at $p$** when $g_i(x)+Dg_i(x)p=0$. For equality multiplier
$\nu$ and inequality multipliers $\lambda\ge0$, a **KKT tuple** for the
subproblem satisfies primal feasibility,
$$Bp+\nabla f(x)+Dh(x)^T\nu+Dg(x)^T\lambda=0, \qquad \lambda_i\bigl(g_i(x)+Dg_i(x)p\bigr)=0\quad(1\le i\le m).$$
Rows of $Dh(x)$ and active rows of $Dg(x)$ are stacked in that order in the
subproblem KKT matrix $\begin{bmatrix}B&A^T\\A&0\end{bmatrix}$.

All inequality signs and multiplier signs here agree with the source program:
$g_i\le0$ and $\lambda_i\ge0$.

Replacing $p$ by $tp$ in that same model gives a distinct finite trial value; the Armijo inequality compares it with the actual nonlinear merit at $x+tp$. This definition supplies a test only and, as stated, implies no positivity or acceptance claim.

citations.quote:
Use the smooth program, dimensions, gradient conventions, and Lagrangian
$L(x,\nu,\lambda)=f(x)+\nu^Th(x)+\lambda^Tg(x)$ of
[[def-inequality-constrained-program-and-kkt-geometry]]. Let $\rho>0$,
$\nu\in\mathbb R^p$, and $\lambda\in\mathbb R^m_+$. The equality
augmented Lagrangian is
$$\mathcal L^E_\rho(x,\nu)=f(x)+\nu^Th(x)+\tfrac{\rho}{2}\|h(x)\|_2^2.$$
For inequalities, with $[z]_i^+=\max\{z_i,0\}$, the projected
(Powell–Hestenes–Rockafellar) augmented Lagrangian is
$$\mathcal L_\rho(x,\nu,\lambda)=f(x)+\nu^Th(x)+\tfrac{\rho}{2}\|h(x)\|_2^2+ \frac{\|[\lambda+\rho g(x)]_+\|_2^2-\|\lambda\|_2^2}{2\rho}.$$
After an inner candidate $x^+$ is produced, the multiplier update is
$$\nu^+=\nu+\rho h(x^+),\qquad \lambda^+=[\lambda+\rho g(x^+)]_+.$$
The bracket is componentwise. A **declared inner stationarity residual** is
$\|\nabla_x\mathcal L_\rho(x^+,\nu,\lambda)\|_2$; an inner procedure must
report the residual it achieved or an explicit failure status.

The equality and inequality formulas are distinct branches. For an inequality
with $\lambda_i+\rho g_i(x)>0$, its summand equals
$\lambda_i g_i(x)+\rho g_i(x)^2/2$; when
$\lambda_i+\rho g_i(x)\le0$, its summand is constant in $x$.

Use the program and dimensions of
[[def-inequality-constrained-program-and-kkt-geometry]]. For any $x\in U$,
$\nu\in\mathbb R^p$, and $\lambda\in\mathbb R^m$, define coordinatewise
$[v]_i^+=\max\{v_i,0\}$ and the scaled residual
$$
r_{\mathrm{KKT}}(x,\nu,\lambda)=\|\nabla f(x)+Dh(x)^T\nu+Dg(x)^T\lambda\|_2+\|h(x)\|_2+\|[g(x)]^+\|_2+\|[-\lambda]^+\|_2+\|\lambda\circ g(x)\|_2.
$$
The symbol $\circ$ denotes coordinatewise multiplication. The norm is the
Euclidean norm from [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and the norm of the
zero-dimensional vector is $0$.

For a convex set $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and $x\in C$, its (outward) normal
cone is
$$
N_C(x)=\{v\in\mathbb R^n:\langle v,y-x\rangle\le0\text{ for every }y\in C\}.
$$
This definition applies in particular when $C$ is closed and convex.

symmetric positive-definite matrix $B\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$. The
**SQP quadratic subproblem** is
$$\min_{p\in\mathbb R^n}\quad \nabla f(x)^Tp+\tfrac12p^TBp \quad\text{subject to}\quad h(x)+Dh(x)p=0,\quad g(x)+Dg(x)p\le0.$$
The variable $p$ is the proposed displacement. Its feasible set is the
polyhedron defined by the displayed affine constraints. A constraint index
$i$ is **active at $p$** when $g_i(x)+Dg_i(x)p=0$. For equality multiplier
$\nu$ and inequality multipliers $\lambda\ge0$, a **KKT tuple** for the
subproblem satisfies primal feasibility,
$$Bp+\nabla f(x)+Dh(x)^T\nu+Dg(x)^T\lambda=0, \qquad \lambda_i\bigl(g_i(x)+Dg_i(x)p\bigr)=0\quad(1\le i\le m).$$
Rows of $Dh(x)$ and active rows of $Dg(x)$ are stacked in that order in the
subproblem KKT matrix $\begin{bmatrix}B&A^T\\A&0\end{bmatrix}$.

All inequality signs and multiplier signs here agree with the source program:
$g_i\le0$ and $\lambda_i\ge0$.

Let $A\in\mathbb R^{r\times n}$ and $b\in\mathbb R^r$. Exactly one of the
following holds:

1. There is $x\in\mathbb R^n$ with $x\ge0$ and $Ax=b$.
2. There is $y\in\mathbb R^r$ with $A^Ty\ge0$ and $b^Ty<0$.

Inequalities between vectors are coordinatewise.

Let $m\ge0$ be an integer. Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and convex,
and suppose the objective $f:U\to\mathbb R$ and inequalities
$g_i:U\to\mathbb R$ $(1\le i\le m)$ are differentiable and convex.
Let the equalities be $Ax=b$ and define the feasible set
$C=\{x\in U:Ax=b,\ g_i(x)\le0\ (1\le i\le m)\}$. If a feasible tuple
$(x_*,\nu,\lambda)$ satisfies the KKT conditions with $\lambda\ge0$, then
$x_*$ is a global minimizer over the feasible set $C$. Moreover,
$-\nabla f(x_*)\in N_C(x_*)$, where the normal cone has the convention of
[[def-kkt-residual-and-normal-cone]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

derivations.claim: If n=0, R^0 is a singleton, so the nonempty feasible set has its unique minimizer there; independence forces the equality matrix to have zero rows, and zero multipliers give the KKT certificate. For n>=1, the unit sphere is compact by [F4]. The continuous function z -> z^T B z is positive on it, so it attains a positive minimum alpha. Thus q(p) >= alpha/2 ||p||_2^2 - ||c||_2 ||p||_2 by [F6], which tends to +infinity as ||p||_2 tends to infinity. By [F1], the constraint rows are affine, so their closed half-spaces and affine equality sets intersect in a closed set; choosing one feasible p_0, the nonempty sublevel {p in C: q(p)<=q(p_0)} is bounded and closed, hence compact by [F4]. The minimum is attained there and therefore on C.

If two distinct feasible points $p_1,p_2$ minimized $q$, their midpoint is feasible and $$q\bigl((p_1+p_2)/2\bigr)=\tfrac12q(p_1)+\tfrac12q(p_2)-\tfrac18(p_1-p_2)^TB(p_1-p_2)<q(p_1),$$ contradicting minimality. Hence the minimizer $p_*$ is unique.

Let $I=\{i:G_ip_*+d_i=0\}$. For any $z$ with $Az=0$ and $G_iz\le0$ for $i\in I$, inactive constraints have positive slack, so for all sufficiently small $t>0$, $p_*+tz\in C$. Minimality and the one-sided derivative at $t=0$ give $(Bp_*+c)^Tz\ge0$. Therefore $v:=-(Bp_*+c)$ satisfies $v^Tz\le0$ for every such $z$.

If $v$ were not representable as $A^T\eta+\sum_{i\in I}\mu_iG_i^T$ with $\mu_i\ge0$, apply [F2] to the matrix whose columns are $G_i^T$ for $i\in I$, the columns of $A^T$, and their negatives, with right-hand side $v$. The alternative gives $y$ with $G_iy\ge0$, $Ay=0$, and $v^Ty<0$. Then $z=-y$ satisfies the direction conditions of step 2.2 but $v^Tz>0$, a contradiction. Thus $v=A^T\eta+\sum_{i\in I}\mu_iG_i^T$ for some $\mu_i\ge0$. Since $v=-(Bp_*+c)$, this is KKT stationarity with equality multiplier $\eta$; setting inactive multipliers to zero gives complementarity.

If $A$ has positive row count, full row rank makes $AA^T$ positive definite, so set $P=I-A^T(AA^T)^{-1}A$; if it has zero rows, set $P=I$. Direct multiplication gives $AP=0$, $P^T=P$, and $P^2=P$, and $Pz=z$ for every $z\in\ker A$. Thus $P$ is the orthogonal projection onto $\ker A$ and $\ker P=\operatorname{range}(A^T)$. Project the multiplier representation from step 3.1. If the projected active normals with positive coefficients are dependent, choose a nonzero dependence, change its sign to give a positive coefficient, and subtract $t$ times that relation, where $t$ is the minimum ratio of a current multiplier to a positive dependence coefficient. All coefficients remain nonnegative and at least one becomes zero. Repeating finitely many times leaves independent projected normals. Their unprojected remainder lies in $\ker P=\operatorname{range}(A^T)$, so it is absorbed into the equality multiplier. If a linear combination of the equality rows and supported active rows is zero, projecting it by $P$ first forces all active coefficients to be zero by projected independence; full row rank then forces the equality coefficients to be zero.

The feasible tuple from steps 3.1–3.1 satisfies the hypotheses of [F3], because $q$ is differentiable and convex and every constraint is affine. Thus it certifies a global minimizer; step 2.1 makes that global minimizer unique.

1. Solve the equality-constrained direction problem

3. If $u\ne0$, for every $i\notin W_k$ with $G_iu>0$ compute

and let $H\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric and positive definite on
$\ker A$: $z^THz>0$ whenever $0\ne z\in\ker A$. Then
$$K=\begin{bmatrix}H&A^T\\A&0\end{bmatrix}$$
is nonsingular. Here the zero-row case $r=0$ is allowed.

Let $q(p)=c^Tp+\tfrac12p^TBp$ on $\mathbb R^n$, where $B=B^T$ is positive
definite. Let the feasible set be the nonempty polyhedron
$$C=\{p:Ap=b,\ G_ip+d_i\le0\ (1\le i\le m)\},$$
where the equality rows of $A$ are linearly independent (zero rows are
allowed). Then $q$ has a unique minimizer $p_*$. There are equality
multipliers $\nu$ and inequality multipliers $\lambda_i\ge0$ such that
$$Bp_*+c+A^T\nu+\sum_i\lambda_iG_i^T=0, \qquad \lambda_i(G_ip_*+d_i)=0.$$

Its KKT equation is $Bu+(Bz+c)+A^T\nu+\sum_{i\in W}\mu_iG_i^T=0$, with $Au=0$ and $G_iu=0$ for $i\in W$. Multiplying by $u^T$ gives $(Bz+c)^Tu=-u^TBu$. Hence for every accepted $0<\alpha\le1$, $$q(z+\alpha u)-q(z)=-\alpha(1-\alpha/2)u^TBu<0.$$ If $\alpha<1$, a blocking row cannot lie in the span of the current rows, since it has $G_iu>0$ while every row in that span annihilates $u$; adding it preserves independence.

Suppose instead $u=0$ and the multiplier of a working inequality $j$ is negative. After deleting $j$, let $v$ be the next exact direction. If $v=0$, the new stationarity equation, extended with a zero multiplier on row $j$, and the old one give two multiplier representations for the same gradient on independent old working rows; uniqueness would force $\mu_j=0$, a contradiction. Hence $v\ne0$. The new direction stationarity, dotted with $v$, gives $(Bz+c)^Tv=-v^TBv$. The old face stationarity, also dotted with $v$, gives $(Bz+c)^Tv+\mu_jG_jv=0$, because all retained working rows annihilate $v$. Therefore $\mu_jG_jv=v^TBv>0$, so $v\ne0$ and $G_jv<0$. Once the algorithm reaches that face minimizer, either all working inequality multipliers are nonnegative and it terminates, or step 1.2 gives a strict objective decrease after a negative multiplier is dropped. Every later iterate is then below the minimum value on that face, so the same working set cannot be face-minimized again. There are at most $2^m$ working sets.

Between successive face minimizers, each nonterminal partial step adds an independent blocker, so there can be at most $n-r$ such additions before the feasible direction space is zero. A full step with no blocker reaches a face minimizer immediately. Thus each of the at most $2^m$ face-minimization episodes uses at most $n-r+2\le n+2$ iterations. The cap $N\ge(n+2)2^m$ cannot be reached before a terminal KKT point.

At termination, feasibility is maintained and every working inequality multiplier is nonnegative; assign zero multipliers to inequalities outside the working set. This is a KKT tuple at a point $z$. the algorithm reports no KKT certificate

Let $c_A:U\to\mathbb R^r$ collect the equality constraints and a specified
set of active inequality constraints, in that order. Given $x,x+p\in U$,
assume $A=Dc_A(x)$ has full row rank and the SQP step satisfies
$c_A(x)+Ap=0$. For $r>0$, compute
$$w=-A^T(AA^T)^{-1}c_A(x+p)$$
and return $p+w$ as the corrected displacement. If the rank test fails,
the inverse or evaluation fails, return `correction-failure`. If $r=0$,
return $p$ with $w=0$. This is a correction for the specified active
constraints; it does not certify feasibility of inactive constraints.

For a $C^2$ scalar field near $a$,

$$f(a+h)=f(a)+\nabla f(a)\cdot h+\frac12\langle H_f(a)h,h\rangle+o(\|h\|^2).$$

derivations.claim: Taylor's formula along $x+tp$ and the bound on $D^2c_A$ give $$c_A(x+p)=c_A(x)+Ap+R_p=R_p,\qquad \|R_p\|_2\le\frac M2\|p\|_2^2.$$ Since $\|A^T(AA^T)^{-1}\|_2=1/s_{\min}(A)\le1/s_0$, [F1] yields $\|w\|_2\le M\|p\|_2^2/(2s_0)$ and $c_A(x+p)+Aw=0$.

Put $y=x+p$. Taylor expansion at $y$ gives $$c_A(y+w)=c_A(y)+Dc_A(y)w+R_w =\bigl(Dc_A(y)-A\bigr)w+R_w,$$ where $\|Dc_A(y)-A\|_2\le M\|p\|_2$ and $\|R_w\|_2\le M\|w\|_2^2/2$. Therefore $$\|c_A(y+w)\|_2\le M\|p\|_2\|w\|_2+\tfrac M2\|w\|_2^2 \le \frac{M^2}{2s_0}\|p\|_2^3+\frac{M^3}{8s_0^2}\|p\|_2^4,$$ which is $O(\|p\|_2^3)$ for small $p$. The minimum-norm assertion is [F1].

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$
be $C^2$. Let $p,m\in\mathbb N$ with zero allowed; when the target
dimension is positive, let $h:U\to\mathbb R^p$ and
$g=(g_1,\ldots,g_m):U\to\mathbb R^m$ be componentwise $C^2$, and when it
is zero use the unique empty map. The $C^2$ convention for positive
dimensions is [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]].
The smooth inequality program is to minimize $f(x)$ subject to
$h(x)=0$ and $g_i(x)\le0$ for every $i$. Its feasible set is
$C=\{x\in U:h(x)=0,\ g_i(x)\le0\ (1\le i\le m)\}$. A feasible point $x_*$ is
a local minimizer if some open neighborhood $V$ of $x_*$ satisfies
$f(x_*)\le f(y)$ for every $y\in C\cap V$.

At a feasible $x$, the active set is
$I(x)=\{i:g_i(x)=0\}$. The Bouligand tangent cone and linearized cone are,
respectively,
$$
T_C(x)=\{d:\exists\,t_k>0,\ t_k\downarrow0,\ d_k\to d,\ x+t_kd_k\in C\},

and
$$

$$
Gradients are column vectors and $Dg_i(x)d=\nabla g_i(x)^Td$.

The linear independence constraint qualification (LICQ) holds at $x$ when the rows of $Dh(x)$ together with
$\{\nabla g_i(x)^T:i\in I(x)\}$ are linearly independent. MFCQ holds at $x$
when $Dh(x)$ has full row rank (its rows are linearly independent) and there is $w\in\ker Dh(x)$ with

$I(x)=\varnothing$. Here full row rank for a matrix with zero rows is
understood vacuously.

The Mangasarian–Fromovitz constraint qualification (MFCQ) is the condition
just stated. The Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) system is the stationarity,
feasibility, dual-feasibility, and complementarity system below.

For $\nu\in\mathbb R^p$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb R^m$, the Lagrangian and KKT
system are
$$
L(x,\nu,\lambda)=f(x)+\nu^Th(x)+\lambda^Tg(x),
$$
$$
h(x)=0,\quad g(x)\le0,\quad \lambda\ge0,\quad \lambda_i g_i(x)=0\ (1\le i\le m),\quad \nabla_xL(x,\nu,\lambda)=0.
$$

$\mathcal K(x,\nu,\lambda)=\mathcal L_C(x)\cap

gradient conventions of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]],
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].

Let $A\in\mathbb R^{r\times n}$ have full row rank, where $0\le r\le n$,

$$K=\begin{bmatrix}H&A^T\\A&0\end{bmatrix}$$

$$F_A(x,\mu)=\binom{\nabla_x L(x,\nu,\lambda_I,0_{I^c})}{c_A(x)},\qquad J_A(x,\mu)=\begin{bmatrix}\nabla^2_{xx}L(x,\nu,\lambda_I,0_{I^c})&Dc_A(x)^T\\Dc_A(x)&0\end{bmatrix}.$$

Let $n\ge0$ be an integer, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$, and
let $x_*\in U$ satisfy $F(x_*)=0$ with $J_*:=DF(x_*)$ invertible. Suppose
$J=DF$ is $L$-Lipschitz on a closed ball of positive radius about $x_*$ contained in $U$. Fix
$\bar\eta\in[0,1)$. For $n=0$ use the zero operator-norm convention
of [[lem-inexact-newton-error-recurrence-under-lipschitz-jacobian]]. Consider any sequence
$$x_{k+1}=x_k+p_k,\qquad J(x_k)p_k+F(x_k)=r_k,\qquad \|r_k\|_2\le\eta_k\|F(x_k)\|_2,$$
with $0\le\eta_k\le\bar\eta$. Define
$\|v\|_*:=\|J_*v\|_2$. There is $\rho>0$ such that, if
$\|x_0-x_*\|_*\le\rho$, every iterate remains in the ball and
$\|x_k-x_*\|_*\le q^k\|x_0-x_*\|_*$ for some $q<1$. Consequently:

1. If $\eta_k\to0$, the iterates converge superlinearly (unless an exact root
   is reached, in which case the exact recurrence remains there).
2. If $\eta_k\le C_\eta\|F(x_k)\|_2$ for a constant $C_\eta$, the iterates
   converge quadratically.

The fixed bound $\bar\eta<1$ gives linear convergence. Since $J_*$ is
invertible, these rates in $\|\cdot\|_*$ are equivalent to the same local
rates in the Euclidean norm. For $F=\nabla f$ with $f\in C^2(U)$ (all ordered partial derivatives
through order two exist and are continuous), $J(x)=\nabla^2 f(x)$, so the
residual is the inexact Newton residual
$\nabla^2 f(x_k)p_k+\nabla f(x_k)$, using the Hessian convention of
[[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]]. This theorem concerns the
unshifted full-step recurrence; it does not assert that a safeguarded
line-search algorithm eventually selects that branch.

derivations.claim: Let $A$ stack equality rows and active inequality rows at $x_*$. For $d\in\ker A$, $d$ is linearly feasible and has zero derivative on every active inequality. Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$
be $C^2$. Let $p,m\in\mathbb N$ with zero allowed; when the target
dimension is positive, let $h:U\to\mathbb R^p$ and
$g=(g_1,\ldots,g_m):U\to\mathbb R^m$ be componentwise $C^2$, and when it
is zero use the unique empty map. The $C^2$ convention for positive
dimensions is [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]].
The smooth inequality program is to minimize $f(x)$ subject to
$h(x)=0$ and $g_i(x)\le0$ for every $i$. Its feasible set is
$C=\{x\in U:h(x)=0,\ g_i(x)\le0\ (1\le i\le m)\}$. A feasible point $x_*$ is
a local minimizer if some open neighborhood $V$ of $x_*$ satisfies
$f(x_*)\le f(y)$ for every $y\in C\cap V$.

At a feasible $x$, the active set is
$I(x)=\{i:g_i(x)=0\}$. The Bouligand tangent cone and linearized cone are,
respectively,
$$
T_C(x)=\{d:\exists\,t_k>0,\ t_k\downarrow0,\ d_k\to d,\ x+t_kd_k\in C\},
$$
and
$$
\mathcal L_C(x)=\{d:Dh(x)d=0,\ Dg_i(x)d\le0\text{ for every }i\in I(x)\}.
$$
Gradients are column vectors and $Dg_i(x)d=\nabla g_i(x)^Td$.

The linear independence constraint qualification (LICQ) holds at $x$ when the rows of $Dh(x)$ together with
$\{\nabla g_i(x)^T:i\in I(x)\}$ are linearly independent. MFCQ holds at $x$
when $Dh(x)$ has full row rank (its rows are linearly independent) and there is $w\in\ker Dh(x)$ with

$I(x)=\varnothing$. Here full row rank for a matrix with zero rows is
understood vacuously.

The Mangasarian–Fromovitz constraint qualification (MFCQ) is the condition

h(x)=0,\quad g(x)\le0,\quad \lambda\ge0,\quad \lambda_i g_i(x)=0\ (1\le i\le m),\quad \nabla_xL(x,\nu,\lambda)=0.
$$

$\mathcal K(x,\nu,\lambda)=\mathcal L_C(x)\cap
\{d:\nabla f(x)^Td=0\}$. These definitions use the differentiability and
gradient conventions of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]],
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].

Let $A\in\mathbb R^{r\times n}$ have full row rank, where $0\le r\le n$,

Let $c_A(x)$ stack the equality and identified active constraints, and let

$$P=I-A^T(AA^T)^{-1}A$$

exact Lagrangian Hessian $H$ and a symmetric positive-definite full-memory
BFGS matrix $B$, define
$$H_{\rm red}=H+P(B-H)P.$$

right-hand side $-F_A(x,\mu)$ as in
[[alg-sqp-exact-hessian-newton-step]]. If the rows are dependent or the
solve fails, return `kkt-solve-failure`.

For a curvature pair $(s,y)$ with $s^Ty>0$, the optional next-model update
is
$$B^+=B-\frac{(Bs)(Bs)^T}{s^TBs}+\frac{yy^T}{s^Ty};$$
if $s^Ty\le0$, skip the update and retain $B$. The curvature pair is defined
as in [[def-bfgs-curvature-pair-and-update-formulas]].

derivations.claim: Set $z_k=(x_k,\mu_k)$ and $F_k=F(z_k)$ for the active KKT map. The exact Jacobian $J_k=DF(z_k)$ has upper-left block $H_k$. By [F3], the computed step $s_k=(p_k,\delta\mu_k)$ solves $\widetilde J_ks_k=-F_k$, where $\widetilde J_k$ differs from $J_k$ only by replacing that block with $H_k+P_k(B_k-H_k)P_k$. Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$
be $C^2$. Let $p,m\in\mathbb N$ with zero allowed; when the target
dimension is positive, let $h:U\to\mathbb R^p$ and
$g=(g_1,\ldots,g_m):U\to\mathbb R^m$ be componentwise $C^2$, and when it
is zero use the unique empty map. The $C^2$ convention for positive
dimensions is [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]].
The smooth inequality program is to minimize $f(x)$ subject to
$h(x)=0$ and $g_i(x)\le0$ for every $i$. Its feasible set is
$C=\{x\in U:h(x)=0,\ g_i(x)\le0\ (1\le i\le m)\}$. A feasible point $x_*$ is
a local minimizer if some open neighborhood $V$ of $x_*$ satisfies
$f(x_*)\le f(y)$ for every $y\in C\cap V$.

At a feasible $x$, the active set is
$I(x)=\{i:g_i(x)=0\}$. The Bouligand tangent cone and linearized cone are,
respectively,
$$
T_C(x)=\{d:\exists\,t_k>0,\ t_k\downarrow0,\ d_k\to d,\ x+t_kd_k\in C\},
$$
and
$$
\mathcal L_C(x)=\{d:Dh(x)d=0,\ Dg_i(x)d\le0\text{ for every }i\in I(x)\}.
$$
Gradients are column vectors and $Dg_i(x)d=\nabla g_i(x)^Td$.

The linear independence constraint qualification (LICQ) holds at $x$ when the rows of $Dh(x)$ together with
$\{\nabla g_i(x)^T:i\in I(x)\}$ are linearly independent. MFCQ holds at $x$
when $Dh(x)$ has full row rank (its rows are linearly independent) and there is $w\in\ker Dh(x)$ with
$Dg_i(x)w<0$ for every active $i$; the latter condition is vacuous if
$I(x)=\varnothing$. Here full row rank for a matrix with zero rows is
understood vacuously.

The Mangasarian–Fromovitz constraint qualification (MFCQ) is the condition
just stated. The Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) system is the stationarity,
feasibility, dual-feasibility, and complementarity system below.

For $\nu\in\mathbb R^p$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb R^m$, the Lagrangian and KKT
system are
$$
L(x,\nu,\lambda)=f(x)+\nu^Th(x)+\lambda^Tg(x),
$$
$$
h(x)=0,\quad g(x)\le0,\quad \lambda\ge0,\quad \lambda_i g_i(x)=0\ (1\le i\le m),\quad \nabla_xL(x,\nu,\lambda)=0.
$$
The critical cone for a KKT tuple is
$\mathcal K(x,\nu,\lambda)=\mathcal L_C(x)\cap
\{d:\nabla f(x)^Td=0\}$. These definitions use the differentiability and
gradient conventions of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]],
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].

Use the smooth program, dimensions, gradient conventions, and Lagrangian
$L(x,\nu,\lambda)=f(x)+\nu^Th(x)+\lambda^Tg(x)$ of
[[def-inequality-constrained-program-and-kkt-geometry]]. Let $\rho>0$,
$\nu\in\mathbb R^p$, and $\lambda\in\mathbb R^m_+$. The equality
augmented Lagrangian is
$$\mathcal L^E_\rho(x,\nu)=f(x)+\nu^Th(x)+\tfrac{\rho}{2}\|h(x)\|_2^2.$$
For inequalities, with $[z]_i^+=\max\{z_i,0\}$, the projected
(Powell–Hestenes–Rockafellar) augmented Lagrangian is
$$\mathcal L_\rho(x,\nu,\lambda)=f(x)+\nu^Th(x)+\tfrac{\rho}{2}\|h(x)\|_2^2+ \frac{\|[\lambda+\rho g(x)]_+\|_2^2-\|\lambda\|_2^2}{2\rho}.$$
After an inner candidate $x^+$ is produced, the multiplier update is
$$\nu^+=\nu+\rho h(x^+),\qquad \lambda^+=[\lambda+\rho g(x^+)]_+.$$
The bracket is componentwise. A **declared inner stationarity residual** is
$\|\nabla_x\mathcal L_\rho(x^+,\nu,\lambda)\|_2$; an inner procedure must
report the residual it achieved or an explicit failure status.

The equality and inequality formulas are distinct branches. For an inequality
with $\lambda_i+\rho g_i(x)>0$, its summand equals
$\lambda_i g_i(x)+\rho g_i(x)^2/2$; when
$\lambda_i+\rho g_i(x)\le0$, its summand is constant in $x$.

Let $m,n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{m+n}$ be open, and let
$F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$.  Suppose $(a,b)\in U$, $F(a,b)=0$, and the
**partial derivative in the second block**

$$D_yF(a,b):\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n,\qquad D_yF(a,b)v:=DF(a,b)(0,v),$$

is invertible.  Put similarly $D_xF(a,b)u:=DF(a,b)(u,0)$.  Then there are open
neighbourhoods $P$ of $a$ and $Q$ of $b$, and a unique $C^1$ map
$\varphi:P\to Q$, such that

$$F(x,y)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y=\varphi(x)\qquad((x,y)\in P\times Q).$$

After shrinking $P,Q$ if necessary, $D_yF(x,\varphi(x))$ is invertible and

$$D\varphi(x)=-D_yF(x,\varphi(x))^{-1}D_xF(x,\varphi(x)).$$

Fix a smooth program as in
[[def-sqp-augmented-lagrangian-equality-and-inequality]], a penalty
$\rho>0$, finite outer cap $K\ge1$, finite per-call inner cap $M\ge1$,
tolerances $\epsilon_k\ge0$, and KKT tolerance $\tau\ge0$. A supplied
finite-budget inner procedure receives
$(x_k,\nu_k,\lambda_k,\rho,\epsilon_k,M)$, performs at most $M$ inner
iterations, and returns one of: `success(x_k^+,\widehat\epsilon_k)` with
$x_k^+\in U$ and
$\widehat\epsilon_k=\|\nabla_x\mathcal L_\rho(x_k^+,\nu_k,\lambda_k)\|_2
\le\epsilon_k$; `budget-exhausted(x_{\rm last},\widehat\epsilon_{\rm last})`
with $x_{\rm last}\in U$ and
$\widehat\epsilon_{\rm last}=
\|\nabla_x\mathcal L_\rho(x_{\rm last},\nu_k,\lambda_k)\|_2$; or
`failure(data)` when it cannot continue or report a residual. Each inner
iteration and report computation is finite, and the procedure returns by its
cap.

Initialize $x_0\in U$, $\nu_0\in\mathbb R^p$, and
$\lambda_0\in\mathbb R^m_+$. For $k=0,\ldots,K-1$:

1. Call the inner procedure with cap $M$. On
   `budget-exhausted(x_{\rm last},\widehat\epsilon_{\rm last})`, return
   `inner-budget-exhausted` with current $(x_k,\nu_k,\lambda_k)$, that point,
   and residual. On `failure(data)`,
   return `inner-failure` with the data. If a purported success reports a
   residual exceeding $\epsilon_k$, return `inner-failure` with the reported
   data. Otherwise store its reported inner residual

At each precision, let the representable set, normal range, and unit roundoff be an instance of [[def-standard-relative-floating-point-model-and-unit-roundoff]] specialized to a finite binary format of integer precision $p\ge2$ and integer normal-exponent bounds $j_{\min}\le j\le j_{\max}$. Its normal values are $\pm m2^{j-p+1}$ for integers $2^{p-1}\le m<2^p$ and $j_{\min}\le j\le j_{\max}$, with $N_{\min}=2^{j_{\min}}$ and $N_{\max}=(2^p-1)2^{j_{\max}-p+1}$. The rounding rule is round-to-nearest, ties-to-even by the parity of the normalized significand. Each precision in a mixed-precision procedure has its own format, range, and valid unit-roundoff bound. On every real exact result that is zero or normal, $\operatorname{fl}$ uses this rule; every other nonzero exact result (subnormal or overflow), NaN, infinity, invalid operation, or division by zero returns range-failure. A real add, subtract, multiply, or divide is one rounded operation. For positive in-range $x$, $\operatorname{fl}(\sqrt{x})$ is correctly rounded to nearest, ties-to-even, and fails unless its result is positive and normal. A real fused multiply-add returns the correctly rounded value of the single exact expression $ab+c$; it is not two operations.

Complex addition and subtraction round real and imaginary components separately. A complex product (a+ib)(c+id) uses four rounded real products ac, bd, ad, bc, then rounded subtraction and addition, for six real operations. Conjugation and sign changes are exact. Scaling and division by a positive real scalar round each complex component separately; no other complex division primitive is used here.

A procedure succeeds only when each exact intermediate is zero or normal and every rounded output is finite; otherwise it returns the first range-failure with its operation or pivot index. For ku<1 write gamma_k=ku/(1-ku). This is a no-underflow success model, not the gradual-underflow model.

Let $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, $m\ge n\ge1$, have full column rank. Successful scaled Householder QR gives the exactly orthonormal reduced representative $\widehat Q$ and computed triangular $\widehat R$ with
$$A+\Delta_Q=\widehat Q\widehat R,\qquad \|\Delta_Q\|_F\le\beta_Q\|A\|_F,\qquad \beta_Q=(1+\kappa_m)^n-1,$$
where $\kappa_m$ is the proved local-step coefficient. Apply the stored reflectors to $b$ by rounded rank-one updates and let $\widehat y$ be the first $n$ coordinates. Set $\beta_b=\beta_Q$. Alternatively, if an explicitly supplied exactly orthonormal $\widehat Q$ has entries admissible as arithmetic inputs and $\widehat y=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat Q^Tb)$ uses sequential rounded dots, set $\beta_b=\sqrt n\,\gamma_m$. Solve $\widehat R\widehat x=\widehat y$ by successful rounded back substitution. Suppose $mu<1$ and $\gamma_{n+3}<1/8$. There exist $\delta b$ and upper triangular $\Delta R$ with
$$(\widehat R+\Delta R)\widehat x=\widehat Q^T(b+\delta b),\qquad \|\delta b\|_2\le\beta_b\|b\|_2,\qquad \|\Delta R\|_F\le\gamma_{n+3}\|\widehat R\|_F.$$
If $\widehat R+\Delta R$ is nonsingular, $\widehat x$ is the unique least-squares solution for $\widetilde A=\widehat Q(\widehat R+\Delta R)$ and $\widetilde b=b+\delta b$. The relative matrix perturbation is at most $\beta_Q+\gamma_{n+3}(1+\beta_Q)$; the right-hand perturbation is at most $\beta_b$. For fixed $m,n$, both perturbation coefficients are $O(u)$. If additionally $\beta_Q\le19\gamma_{n+3}/(1+\gamma_{n+3})$ and $\beta_b\le20\gamma_{n+3}$, both relative data perturbation bounds are at most $20\gamma_{n+3}$. These two coefficient comparisons are additional checks; they do not follow from $mu<1$ and $\gamma_{n+3}<1/8$ alone. Success and nonsingularity are explicit hypotheses.

Let $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$, $x\in\mathbb F^n$, $y\in\mathbb F^m$ have stored real or complex entries, with $m,n\ge1$. Use the operationwise arithmetic model, successful sequential dot products, and $0<u<1$ with $(\max(m,n)-1)u<1$. Define
$$g_k=\frac{1+6u}{1-(k-1)u}-1,\qquad F=\|A\|_F,\quad X=\|x\|_2,\quad Y=\|y\|_2.$$
For $\widehat v=\operatorname{fl}(Ax)$ and $\widehat w=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat v-y)$, put $V=g_nFX$ and $W=V+u(\|\widehat v\|_2+Y)$. Then
$$\|\widehat w-(Ax-y)\|_2\le W.$$
For a stored real $\lambda>0$, also compute $\widehat z=\operatorname{fl}(A^*\widehat w)$, $\widehat l=\operatorname{fl}(\lambda x)$ and $\widehat r=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat z+\widehat l)$, rounding scalar multiplication componentwise. The exact intended normal residual $r=A^*(Ax-y)+\lambda x$ satisfies
$$\|\widehat r-r\|_2\le\rho:=FW+g_mF\|\widehat w\|_2+u\lambda X+u(\|\widehat z\|_2+\|\widehat l\|_2).$$
Norms in these certificates mean exact norms or certified upper bounds. Uncontrolled rounding of the certificate itself is not authorized. The linear bound applies columnwise to certify $\|I-AB\|_2\le\|I-AB\|_F$ from stored basis-solve columns $B$.

Let $A\in\mathbb R^{r\times n}$ have full row rank, where $0\le r\le n$,
and let $H\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric and positive definite on
$\ker A$: $z^THz>0$ whenever $0\ne z\in\ker A$. Then
$$K=\begin{bmatrix}H&A^T\\A&0\end{bmatrix}$$
is nonsingular. Here the zero-row case $r=0$ is allowed.

Let $C=[x\;B]\in\mathbb R^{r\times(q+1)}$, $r\ge1$, $q\ge0$, undergo a successful step of [[alg-scaled-householder-reflector-formation-and-application]], with $0<u<1$ and $ru<1$. Define
$$g_r=\frac{ru}{1-ru},\quad e_r=(1+u)^{r/2+3}-1,\quad d_r=e_r+u(2+e_r),\quad a_r=\frac{1+u}{(1-u)^r}-1,$$
$$c_r=2\bigl((1+a_r)(1+u)^2(1+g_r)-1\bigr),\qquad \kappa_r=\max\{e_r+8d_r,(1+u)c_r+3u\}.$$
There is an exact orthogonal $H$, the identity when $x=0$ and $H(v)=I-2vv^T/(v^Tv)$ otherwise, and a perturbation $E$ such that
$$H(C+E)=C_+,\qquad \|E\|_F\le\kappa_r\|C\|_F.$$
The constants increase with $r$ and are $O(ru)$ for fixed $r$ as $u\to0$. The column overwrite is included. For any real separate block $Y\in\mathbb R^{r\times t}$, $t\ge0$, successful application of the same stored $(v,\widehat\tau)$ without an annihilation overwrite has discrepancy from $H(v)Y$ at most $((1+u)c_r+3u)\|Y\|_F$.

Let $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Input a real active column $x\in\mathbb R^r\subseteq\mathbb F^r$ and trailing block $B\in\mathbb F^{r\times q}$ with entries in the floating-point system, $r\ge1$, $q\ge0$. If every component of $x$ is zero, return the identity action and a copy of $B$, with the active output column set to exact zeros, so that $C_+=[0e_1\;B]$; return $(v=0,\widehat\tau=0,\widehat\alpha=0,C_+)$ marked `identity`. Otherwise compute $s=\max_{1\le i\le r}|x_i|>0$, and then, in increasing $i$, compute $z_i=\operatorname{fl}(x_i/s)$. Initialize $t=0$ and, in increasing $i$, compute $a_i=\operatorname{fl}(z_i z_i)$ followed by $t=\operatorname{fl}(t+a_i)$. Compute $h=\operatorname{fl}(\sqrt t)$ and then $\widehat r=\operatorname{fl}(s h)$. Set $\sigma=1$ if $x_1=0$ and $\sigma=\operatorname{sign}(x_1)$ otherwise, and set $\widehat\alpha=-\sigma\widehat r$ using the exact sign change. Compute $v_1=\operatorname{fl}(x_1-\widehat\alpha)$, then copy $v_i=x_i$ exactly for $i=2,\ldots,r$.

Initialize $w=0$ and, in increasing $i$, compute $a_i=\operatorname{fl}(v_i v_i)$ followed by $w=\operatorname{fl}(w+a_i)$. Then compute $\widehat\tau=\operatorname{fl}(2/w)$. For each column $j=1,\ldots,q$ in increasing order, initialize $d_j=0$ and, in increasing $i$, compute $a_{ij}=\operatorname{fl}(v_i B_{ij})$ followed by $d_j=\operatorname{fl}(d_j+a_{ij})$. After all $d_j$ have been computed, in increasing $i$ compute $p_i=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat\tau v_i)$. Then, in increasing $j$ and within each column in increasing $i$, compute $U_{ij}=\operatorname{fl}(p_i d_j)$ and $\widehat B_{ij}=\operatorname{fl}(B_{ij}-U_{ij})$ in that order. The complete active output is $C_+=[\widehat\alpha e_1\;\widehat B]$, with exact zeros written below its first diagonal entry. If any elementary operation fails, return the first range failure with its stage and indices in the order above. Also return failure if $t$, $\widehat r$, or $w$ is not positive normal, or any intermediate is nonfinite. Otherwise return $(v,\widehat\tau,\widehat\alpha,C_+)$ marked `reflector`. For a separate block $Y\in\mathbb F^{r\times q'}$, $q'\ge0$, apply the stored reflector by computing its sequential column dots in increasing column order, then the vector $p_i=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat\tau v_i)$ in increasing $i$, and then each rounded product and subtraction by increasing column and row; omit the target-column overwrite. Store reflector factors with their identity/reflector marker to represent the exact orthogonal product; a rounded explicit dense product is a separate output with its own arithmetic error. For a nonzero stored $v$, the associated exact reflector is $H(v)=I-2vv^T/(v^Tv)$, using [[def-householder-reflector]] and the QR convention of [[def-full-reduced-and-column-pivoted-computational-qr-factorisations]]. Since $v$ is real, this matrix acts on $\mathbb F^r$ as an orthogonal reflector over $\mathbb R$ and a unitary reflector over $\mathbb C$. This definition does not assert a local backward-error bound.

Let $F$ be a field, let $n\ge 1$, and let $b\in F^n$.

If $L=(\ell_{ij})\in M_n(F)$ is lower triangular with every diagonal entry
$\ell_{ii}\ne 0$, the **forward substitution solve** of $Lx=b$ is the recursive
construction

$$x_i:=\frac{1}{\ell_{ii}}\left(b_i-\sum_{j<i}\ell_{ij}x_j\right)\qquad(0\le i<n).$$If $U=(u_{ij})\in M_n(F)$ is upper triangular with every diagonal entry $u_{ii}\ne 0$, the **backward substitution solve** of $Ux=b$ is the recursive construction$$x_i:=\frac{1}{u_{ii}}\left(b_i-\sum_{j>i}u_{ij}x_j\right)\qquad(n-1\ge i\ge 0).$$

The triangular vocabulary is from
[[def-triangular-and-diagonal-matrices-over-a-commutative-ring]]. The matrix
product convention from [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]] is the one
used when later items rewrite these recursions as matrix equations.

At $x\in U$, choose a positive-definite SQP model matrix and solve the exact
quadratic subproblem by
[[alg-sqp-exhaustive-active-set-qp-solve]]. If it reports infeasibility or
failure, return that status. On a solution return, retain its step $p$, full
QP multiplier vectors $(\nu^{QP},\lambda^{QP})$, retained equality basis
$E$, and selected inequality support $J$. The stacked rows $Dh_E(x)$ and
$Dg_J(x)$ are independent, and the selected rows satisfy
$h_E(x)+Dh_E(x)p=0$ and $g_J(x)+Dg_J(x)p=0$. Given parameters $\rho_0>0$,
$\gamma>1$, $\beta\in(0,1)$, $\sigma\in(0,1)$ and finite integer caps
$R,J_{\max}\ge1$, keep the resulting step $p$ fixed, initialize flags
$P_{\rm pos}=\mathrm{false}$ and $P_{\rm dom}=\mathrm{false}$, and perform
attempts $r=0,\ldots,R-1$ with $\rho_r=\rho_0\gamma^r$:

1. Compute $D_r=D_{\rho_r}(x,p)$ from
   [[def-sqp-l1-exact-penalty-merit]]. If $D_r\le0$, go to the next penalty.
   Otherwise set $P_{\rm pos}=\mathrm{true}$.
2. If $x+p\in U$, call
   [[alg-sqp-second-order-correction]] with the specified map
   $c_A=(h_E,g_J)$. If it returns a correction $w$ and $x+p+w\in U$, set
   $P_{\rm dom}=\mathrm{true}$ and test
   $\psi_{\rho_r}(x+p+w)\le\psi_{\rho_r}(x)-\sigma D_r$. If it passes,
   return `accepted-soc` with $x+p+w$, $p$, $(\nu^{QP},\lambda^{QP})$, $E$,
   and $J$. If $x+p\notin U$, skip the correction call.
3. For $j=0,\ldots,J_{\max}-1$, set $t_j=\beta^j$. Whenever $x+t_jp\in U$,
   set $P_{\rm dom}=\mathrm{true}$ and test
   $$\psi_{\rho_r}(x+t_jp)\le\psi_{\rho_r}(x)-\sigma t_jD_r.$$
   On the first passing test, return `accepted` with $x+t_jp$, $t_j$,
   $p$, $(\nu^{QP},\lambda^{QP})$, $E$, and $J$.

After all attempts, if $P_{\rm pos}$ is false, return
`nonpositive-predicted-decrease-budget`. If $P_{\rm pos}$ is true but
$P_{\rm dom}$ is false, return `domain-exit`: no SOC or ordinary trial could
be evaluated in $U$. Otherwise return `line-search-budget-exhausted`. These
finite tests do not guarantee acceptance or convergence.

Use the smooth nonlinear program convention of
[[def-inequality-constrained-program-and-kkt-geometry]]: minimize a $C^2$
objective $f:U\to\mathbb R$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, subject to
$h(x)=0$ and componentwise $g(x)\le0$. Fix a current point $x\in U$ and a
symmetric positive-definite matrix $B\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$. The
**SQP quadratic subproblem** is
$$\min_{p\in\mathbb R^n}\quad \nabla f(x)^Tp+\tfrac12p^TBp \quad\text{subject to}\quad h(x)+Dh(x)p=0,\quad g(x)+Dg(x)p\le0.$$
The variable $p$ is the proposed displacement. Its feasible set is the
polyhedron defined by the displayed affine constraints. A constraint index
$i$ is **active at $p$** when $g_i(x)+Dg_i(x)p=0$. For equality multiplier
$\nu$ and inequality multipliers $\lambda\ge0$, a **KKT tuple** for the
subproblem satisfies primal feasibility,
$$Bp+\nabla f(x)+Dh(x)^T\nu+Dg(x)^T\lambda=0, \qquad \lambda_i\bigl(g_i(x)+Dg_i(x)p\bigr)=0\quad(1\le i\le m).$$
Rows of $Dh(x)$ and active rows of $Dg(x)$ are stacked in that order in the
subproblem KKT matrix $\begin{bmatrix}B&A^T\\A&0\end{bmatrix}$.

All inequality signs and multiplier signs here agree with the source program:
$g_i\le0$ and $\lambda_i\ge0$.

Input an SQP subproblem from [[def-sqp-linearized-quadratic-subproblem]],
using exact real arithmetic. First reduce the linearized equality system
$A_Ep=b_E$: test consistency, and, if consistent, retain the
lexicographically first maximal independent set $E$ of equality row indices
with their right-hand sides. If it is inconsistent, return
`QP-infeasible`.

For each subset $J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}$ in increasing bit-mask order:

1. Stack the retained equality rows and the inequality rows $G_i$ for $i\in J$.
   If these rows are dependent, skip $J$.
2. Treat the selected inequalities as equalities $G_ip=-d_i$ and solve
   $$\begin{bmatrix}B&A_J^T\\A_J&0\end{bmatrix} \binom{p}{\eta}=\binom{-c}{b_J},$$
   where $c=\nabla f(x)$, $A_J$ is the stacked matrix with equality rows $E$
   followed by selected inequality rows $J$, and $b_J$ is the right-hand side
   in that same row order. The multiplier vector $\eta$ is stored in this row
   order. The KKT matrix is
   nonsingular by [[lem-sqp-kkt-matrix-nonsingularity-under-reduced-curvature]].
3. Discard the candidate if any linearized inequality is violated or any
   selected inequality multiplier is negative. Otherwise store $(p,\eta,J)$.

If no candidate is stored, return `QP-infeasible`. Otherwise return the
stored candidate with least quadratic objective, breaking an exact tie by the
least subset bit mask, as `solution(p, nu, lambda, E, J)`. Here $\nu$ is
the full equality-multiplier vector, initialized to zero and filled from the
equality components of $\eta$ at indices $E$; $\lambda$ is the full
inequality-multiplier vector, initialized to zero and filled from the selected
components at indices $J$. A finite-precision
implementation that cannot complete a rank test or solve must return
`numerical-failure`; this definition's exact-arithmetic branch has no such
failure. The loop tests at most $2^m$ inequality subsets. It requires no
feasible initial step and specifies no pivoting rule for an iterative working
set solver.

For the SQP subproblem of [[def-sqp-linearized-quadratic-subproblem]] with
$B$ symmetric positive definite, the exact algorithm of
[[alg-sqp-exhaustive-active-set-qp-solve]] terminates after finitely many
subset tests. It returns `QP-infeasible` exactly when the subproblem's
polyhedron is empty; otherwise it returns the unique global minimizer, full
equality and inequality multiplier vectors, and the retained equality basis
$E$ and inequality support $J$ of its KKT certificate.

Let $m\ge0$ be an integer. Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and convex,
and suppose the objective $f:U\to\mathbb R$ and inequalities
$g_i:U\to\mathbb R$ $(1\le i\le m)$ are differentiable and convex.
Let the equalities be $Ax=b$ and define the feasible set
$C=\{x\in U:Ax=b,\ g_i(x)\le0\ (1\le i\le m)\}$. If a feasible tuple
$(x_*,\nu,\lambda)$ satisfies the KKT conditions with $\lambda\ge0$, then
$x_*$ is a global minimizer over the feasible set $C$. Moreover,
$-\nabla f(x_*)\in N_C(x_*)$, where the normal cone has the convention of
[[def-kkt-residual-and-normal-cone]].

derivations.claim: At $x_0$, $\nabla f(x_0)=0$ and the linearized inequality is $1-p_1-p_2\le0$. The unconstrained minimizer $p=0$ is infeasible. On the active face $p_1+p_2=1$, stationarity for $q(p)=\tfrac12\|p\|_2^2$ is $p-\lambda(1,1)^T=0$; combining with the face equation gives $p_1=p_2=\lambda=1/2$. This point is feasible with nonnegative multiplier.
The positive-definite QP has a unique minimizer; its feasible KKT tuple passes the active-set acceptance filters in [F2]. By [F3] the returned step is exactly $(1/2,1/2)$.

The nonlinear point $x_*=(1/2,1/2)$ is feasible and has $\nabla f(x_*)=(1/2,1/2)$, $\nabla g(x_*)=(-1,-1)$, and multiplier $\lambda_*=1/2$. Thus stationarity holds, the multiplier is nonnegative, and complementarity holds with $g(x_*)=0$. Since the objective is convex and the constraint affine, [F4] proves global optimality; strict convexity of the objective makes the minimizer unique.

$$D_\rho(x,p)=-\left[\nabla f(x)^Tp+\rho\left(\|h(x)+Dh(x)p\|_1-\|h(x)\|_1+ \|[g(x)+Dg(x)p]_+\|_1-\|[g(x)]_+\|_1\right)\right].$$
A trial fraction $t\in(0,1]$ satisfies the Armijo test with coefficient
$\sigma\in(0,1)$ when
$$\psi_\rho(x+tp)\le\psi_\rho(x)-\sigma tD_\rho(x,p).$$
The definition alone does not assert $D_\rho(x,p)>0$, existence of an
accepted fraction, or convergence of a sequence of accepted SQP steps.

Let $c_A:U\to\mathbb R^r$ collect the equality constraints and a specified
set of active inequality constraints, in that order. Given $x,x+p\in U$,
assume $A=Dc_A(x)$ has full row rank and the SQP step satisfies
$c_A(x)+Ap=0$. For $r>0$, compute
$$w=-A^T(AA^T)^{-1}c_A(x+p)$$
and return $p+w$ as the corrected displacement. If the rank test fails,
the inverse or evaluation fails, return `correction-failure`. If $r=0$,
return $p$ with $w=0$. This is a correction for the specified active
constraints; it does not certify feasibility of inactive constraints.

Let $c_A:U\to\mathbb R^r$ with $r\ge1$ be $C^2$ on a convex ball about $x$, and assume
$\|D^2c_A(z)[u,v]\|_2\le M\|u\|_2\|v\|_2$ throughout that ball. Let
$A=Dc_A(x)$ have smallest singular value at least $s_0>0$, and let $p$ be
small enough that $x+p$ and the correction segment stay in the ball. If
$c_A(x)+Ap=0$ and $w$ is the correction of
[[alg-sqp-second-order-correction]], then
$$\|w\|_2\le\frac{M}{2s_0}\|p\|_2^2, \qquad \|c_A(x+p+w)\|_2=O(\|p\|_2^3)\quad(p\to0).$$
The correction is the unique minimum-norm vector satisfying
$Aw=-c_A(x+p)$.

At $x\in U$, choose a positive-definite SQP model matrix and solve the exact
quadratic subproblem by
[[alg-sqp-exhaustive-active-set-qp-solve]]. If it reports infeasibility or
failure, return that status. On a solution return, retain its step $p$, full
QP multiplier vectors $(\nu^{QP},\lambda^{QP})$, retained equality basis
$E$, and selected inequality support $J$. The stacked rows $Dh_E(x)$ and
$Dg_J(x)$ are independent, and the selected rows satisfy
$h_E(x)+Dh_E(x)p=0$ and $g_J(x)+Dg_J(x)p=0$. Given parameters $\rho_0>0$,
$\gamma>1$, $\beta\in(0,1)$, $\sigma\in(0,1)$ and finite integer caps
$R,J_{\max}\ge1$, keep the resulting step $p$ fixed, initialize flags
$P_{\rm pos}=\mathrm{false}$ and $P_{\rm dom}=\mathrm{false}$, and perform
attempts $r=0,\ldots,R-1$ with $\rho_r=\rho_0\gamma^r$:

1. Compute $D_r=D_{\rho_r}(x,p)$ from
   [[def-sqp-l1-exact-penalty-merit]]. If $D_r\le0$, go to the next penalty.
   Otherwise set $P_{\rm pos}=\mathrm{true}$.
2. If $x+p\in U$, call
   [[alg-sqp-second-order-correction]] with the specified map
   $c_A=(h_E,g_J)$. If it returns a correction $w$ and $x+p+w\in U$, set
   $P_{\rm dom}=\mathrm{true}$ and test
   $\psi_{\rho_r}(x+p+w)\le\psi_{\rho_r}(x)-\sigma D_r$. If it passes,
   return `accepted-soc` with $x+p+w$, $p$, $(\nu^{QP},\lambda^{QP})$, $E$,
   and $J$. If $x+p\notin U$, skip the correction call.
3. For $j=0,\ldots,J_{\max}-1$, set $t_j=\beta^j$. Whenever $x+t_jp\in U$,
   set $P_{\rm dom}=\mathrm{true}$ and test
   $$\psi_{\rho_r}(x+t_jp)\le\psi_{\rho_r}(x)-\sigma t_jD_r.$$
   On the first passing test, return `accepted` with $x+t_jp$, $t_j$,
   $p$, $(\nu^{QP},\lambda^{QP})$, $E$, and $J$.

After all attempts, if $P_{\rm pos}$ is false, return
`nonpositive-predicted-decrease-budget`. If $P_{\rm pos}$ is true but
$P_{\rm dom}$ is false, return `domain-exit`: no SOC or ordinary trial could
be evaluated in $U$. Otherwise return `line-search-budget-exhausted`. These
finite tests do not guarantee acceptance or convergence.

abla f(x)=4(c,s)-(1,0)$. The unit tangent $t=(-s,c)$ satisfies $t^T
abla f(x)=s$. The QP constraint gives $p\in\operatorname{span}(t)$; minimizing $
abla f(x)^Tp+	frac12\|p\|_2^2$ on this line gives $p=-st=(s^2,-sc)$. Its QP multiplier is $-(4-c)/2$, since $p+
abla f(x)=(4-c)(c,s)$.

Here $Dh(x)Dh(x)^T=4$, so [F3] gives $w=(-cs^2/2,-s^3/2)$ and $\|w\|_2=s^2/2$. Direct substitution into the quadratic constraint yields $$h(x+p+w)=\frac{s^4}{4}.$$ The corrected first coordinate is $c+s^2(1-c/2)$, so the corrected objective change is $-s^2(1-c/2)+s^4/2$. Adding the penalty contribution gives $$\psi_\rho(x+p+w)-\psi_\rho(x) =-s^2(1-c/2)+s^4(1/2+\rho/4).$$

Since $x^Tp=0$ and $\|p\|_2^2=s^2$, $h(x+p)=s^2$. Also $\nabla f(x)^Tp=-s^2$, so [F2] gives $D_\rho=s^2$. The objective changes by $s^2$, while the equality violation changes from zero to $s^2$; hence the full-step merit change is $(1+\rho)s^2>0$, which fails the Armijo right side $-\sigma s^2<0$.

Divide the corrected merit change plus $\sigma D_\rho$ by $s^2$. With $\sigma=1/4$, the result is $-1+c/2+s^2(1/2+\rho/4)+1/4$, which tends to $-1/4$ as $\theta\to0$. It is therefore negative for all sufficiently small nonzero $\theta$, proving the SOC Armijo test passes. citations.quote:
Use the smooth program, dimensions, gradient conventions, and Lagrangian
$L(x,\nu,\lambda)=f(x)+\nu^Th(x)+\lambda^Tg(x)$ of
[[def-inequality-constrained-program-and-kkt-geometry]]. Let $\rho>0$,
$\nu\in\mathbb R^p$, and $\lambda\in\mathbb R^m_+$. The equality
augmented Lagrangian is
$$\mathcal L^E_\rho(x,\nu)=f(x)+\nu^Th(x)+\tfrac{\rho}{2}\|h(x)\|_2^2.$$
For inequalities, with $[z]_i^+=\max\{z_i,0\}$, the projected
(Powell–Hestenes–Rockafellar) augmented Lagrangian is
$$\mathcal L_\rho(x,\nu,\lambda)=f(x)+\nu^Th(x)+\tfrac{\rho}{2}\|h(x)\|_2^2+ \frac{\|[\lambda+\rho g(x)]_+\|_2^2-\|\lambda\|_2^2}{2\rho}.$$
After an inner candidate $x^+$ is produced, the multiplier update is
$$\nu^+=\nu+\rho h(x^+),\qquad \lambda^+=[\lambda+\rho g(x^+)]_+.$$
The bracket is componentwise. A **declared inner stationarity residual** is
$\|\nabla_x\mathcal L_\rho(x^+,\nu,\lambda)\|_2$; an inner procedure must
report the residual it achieved or an explicit failure status.

The equality and inequality formulas are distinct branches. For an inequality
with $\lambda_i+\rho g_i(x)>0$, its summand equals
$\lambda_i g_i(x)+\rho g_i(x)^2/2$; when
$\lambda_i+\rho g_i(x)\le0$, its summand is constant in $x$.

Fix a smooth program as in
[[def-sqp-augmented-lagrangian-equality-and-inequality]], a penalty
$\rho>0$, finite outer cap $K\ge1$, finite per-call inner cap $M\ge1$,
tolerances $\epsilon_k\ge0$, and KKT tolerance $\tau\ge0$. A supplied
finite-budget inner procedure receives
$(x_k,\nu_k,\lambda_k,\rho,\epsilon_k,M)$, performs at most $M$ inner
iterations, and returns one of: `success(x_k^+,\widehat\epsilon_k)` with
$x_k^+\in U$ and
$\widehat\epsilon_k=\|\nabla_x\mathcal L_\rho(x_k^+,\nu_k,\lambda_k)\|_2
\le\epsilon_k$; `budget-exhausted(x_{\rm last},\widehat\epsilon_{\rm last})`
with $x_{\rm last}\in U$ and
$\widehat\epsilon_{\rm last}=
\|\nabla_x\mathcal L_\rho(x_{\rm last},\nu_k,\lambda_k)\|_2$; or
`failure(data)` when it cannot continue or report a residual. Each inner
iteration and report computation is finite, and the procedure returns by its
cap.

Initialize $x_0\in U$, $\nu_0\in\mathbb R^p$, and
$\lambda_0\in\mathbb R^m_+$. For $k=0,\ldots,K-1$:

1. Call the inner procedure with cap $M$. On
   `budget-exhausted(x_{\rm last},\widehat\epsilon_{\rm last})`, return
   `inner-budget-exhausted` with current $(x_k,\nu_k,\lambda_k)$, that point,
   and residual. On `failure(data)`,
   return `inner-failure` with the data. If a purported success reports a
   residual exceeding $\epsilon_k$, return `inner-failure` with the reported
   data. Otherwise store its reported inner residual
   $\widehat\epsilon_k$.
2. Set
   $$\nu_{k+1}=\nu_k+\rho h(x_k^+),\qquad \lambda_{k+1}=[\lambda_k+\rho g(x_k^+)]_+.$$
3. Set $r_k=r_{\rm KKT}(x_k^+,\nu_{k+1},\lambda_{k+1})$. If $r_k\le\tau$,
   return `kkt-tolerance-reached` with $x_k^+$, $(\nu_{k+1},\lambda_{k+1})$,
   $r_k$, and $\widehat\epsilon_k$; otherwise set $x_{k+1}=x_k^+$ and
   continue.

If all $K$ outer iterations finish without that test passing, return
`outer-budget-exhausted` with $x_K$, $(\nu_K,\lambda_K)$, the last KKT
residual $r_{K-1}$, and inner residual $\widehat\epsilon_{K-1}$. The routine
claims neither convergence nor that the inner procedure succeeds within its
cap.
